questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Arc Length of a Smooth Curve Using the Arc Length Formula
questions.problem: Compute the arc length of $y=\frac{2}{3}{({x}^{2}+1)}^{3/2}$ for $x\in [1,4].$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{2}{3}{({x}^{2}+1)}^{3/2},$ $a=1,$ and $b=4.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{({x}^{2}+1)}^{1/2}\cdot 2x=2x\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{[2x\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)}]}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4{x}^{4}+4{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =2{x}^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=2{x}^{2}+1$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(2{x}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+x)|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =[\frac{2}{3}(4)^{3}+(4)]-[\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3}+(1)] \\  & =45.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Representation For an Arc Length
questions.problem: Which of the following gives the length of the curve $y=\frac{1}{9}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{3/2}$ on $[0,3]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{1}{9}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{3/2},$ $a=0,$ and $b=3.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{9}(\frac{3}{2})6{x}^{2}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{1/2}={x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1}
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)={x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{({x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}(2{x}^{3}+1)}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+2{x}^{7}+{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{2{x}^{7}+{x}^{4}+1}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying a Possible Curve Given Its Arc Length As an Integral
questions.problem: The length of a curve $y=f(x)$ is given by ${\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.$ Which of the following could be  an equation for this curve?
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm \frac{1}{1-x}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm \int \frac{1}{1-x}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm (-\operatorname{ln}⁡|1-x|)+C \\  & =\pm \operatorname{ln}⁡(1-x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-x)+7.$

questions.problem: The length of a curve $y=f(x)$ is given by ${\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{1+400{x}^{6}}\,\text{d}x.$ Which of the following could be  an equation for this curve?
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{1+400{x}^{6}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=400{x}^{6}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm 20{x}^{3}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm 20\int {x}^{3}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm 5{x}^{4}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=-5{x}^{4}+2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Arc Length of a Smooth Curve Using the Arc Length Formula
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x),$ $a=1,$ and $b=2.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{x}{4}-\frac{1}{x}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x}{4}-\frac{1}{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+(\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+8{x}^{2}+16}{16{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{2}}{16{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{x}{4}+\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x)|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{{2}^{2}}{8}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2]-[\frac{{1}^{2}}{8}+\operatorname{ln}⁡1] \\  & =\frac{3}{8}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$
